headline: SEBI's GARUDA Framework Slashes AIF Launch Timelines, Clearing a Key Bottleneck for Startup Investors
subheadline: India's market regulator approves a green-channel mechanism that cuts Alternative Investment Fund scheme launches from 30 days to as few as 10, with accredited-investor funds eligible for immediate launch.
body:
• SEBI's GARUDA framework cuts AIF scheme launch timelines from 30 days to 10 working days, enabling faster capital deployment into Indian startups.
  • Funds targeting only accredited investors and angel funds can now launch immediately upon filing — no waiting period at all.
  • The reform shifts India's AIF regime from pre-approval scrutiny to a disclosure-led, post-facto supervision model aligned with global norms.
  • For NRI and diaspora investors routing capital through AIFs, faster fund launches mean quicker access to India's startup ecosystem.

India's capital markets regulator has cleared a significant bottleneck for the country's venture capital and private equity industry. At its board meeting on 19 June 2026, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) approved the GARUDA framework — short for Green-Channel: AIF Rollout Upon Document Acknowledgement — overhauling how Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) launch new schemes.

The change is structural: SEBI is moving from a pre-clearance model, where every fund scheme sat in a regulatory queue for up to 30 days, to a disclosure-led regime where accountability rests squarely on fund managers.

How GARUDA Works

Previously, an AIF had to file its Private Placement Memorandum (PPM) — the principal disclosure document detailing investment strategy, fees, risks, and governance — through a merchant banker, then wait 30 days before launching. GARUDA compresses that along two tracks.

For regular schemes, the launch window shrinks to 10 working days after filing, unless SEBI raises objections. For an AIF's first scheme, launch is permitted from the date of registration or 10 working days from filing, whichever comes later.

The deeper relaxation applies to Accredited Investor-only (AI-only) schemes and Angel Funds. These no longer need a merchant banker. Instead, the AIF manager's CEO and compliance officer submit an undertaking directly to SEBI, and the scheme can launch immediately — a zero-waiting-period regime.

Faster Capital Into Startups

In a market where VC deals close in weeks, a 30-day regulatory lag meant fund managers sat on committed capital they couldn't deploy. For early-stage startups competing for runway, that delay could mean losing a round to a faster-moving competitor.

"Even if funds could raise the requisite capital from the market, they couldn't really deploy anything till the vehicle was set up, leading to delays of deploying capital into startups," said Archana Jahagirdar, Founder and Managing Partner at Rukam Capital.

Pranav Pai, managing partner at 3one4 Capital, drew a comparison with global norms: "In most mature markets, once the manager is licensed and the investors are accredited, the emphasis is on disclosures and accountability rather than repeated approvals. GARUDA moves India towards that approach."

The Numbers

The reform arrives as India's alternative investment sector scales rapidly. Registered AIFs have surged to 1,849 as of March 2026 — up from 732 five years ago. Cumulative commitments stand at ₹15.74 lakh crore ($188 billion), with net investments at ₹6.45 lakh crore ($77 billion) as of December 2025. Accredited investors alone held AIF units worth approximately ₹1.91 lakh crore, nearly 30% of total investments.

What It Means for Diaspora Investors

For NRI and overseas Indian investors, AIFs have become an increasingly popular vehicle to access India's startup economy. But cross-border investors face compounded friction: foreign exchange compliance, FEMA regulations, and — until now — lengthy fund launch timelines.

GARUDA addresses the last of those. Jahagirdar noted that foreign investors had "often found it difficult to understand the time involved in launching AIF schemes in India," and that a predictable process could "facilitate greater foreign capital inflows and encourage increased participation through AIFs."

The Trade-Off

The shift is not without risk. By reducing upfront vetting, SEBI is betting that post-facto enforcement — scrutiny on a sample and risk basis after launch — will catch irregularities. Fund managers now bear direct liability for misstatements or incomplete disclosures.

"Fund managers still need to comply with a large number of regulatory requirements," cautioned Anil Joshi, managing partner at Unicorn India Ventures. "If some of the non-essential compliances can be eased, it would be particularly beneficial for smaller funds."

GARUDA may not resolve every friction point in India's alternative investment landscape, but it removes one that had long frustrated the industry. Whether the reform translates into faster startup funding will depend on execution — by fund managers navigating the new regime and by SEBI enforcing accountability on the back end.
diaspora_angle: NRI and overseas Indian investors increasingly use AIFs to access India's startup ecosystem. GARUDA removes a key friction point — lengthy fund launch timelines — that compounded the complexity of cross-border investing through these vehicles. Faster, more predictable launches should encourage greater diaspora capital inflows.
